claims.text: Controlled thermal aging promotes fine, coherent nanoprecipitates within the lamellar microstructure of a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Such nanoprecipitation-producing aging will simultaneously increase strength and ductility relative to the as-cast state.
The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has a lamellar microstructure of alternating soft FCC and hard B2/BCC phases.
A sub-solvus aging treatment at approximately 700–800 °C can induce nucleation and growth of coherent nanoprecipitates at eutectic phase interfaces.
Keeping the treatment below the precipitate-coarsening temperature will preserve nanoscale precipitate dimensions and coherency.
The treatment will produce a uniform distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates along the eutectic lamellar interfaces.
The nanoprecipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby cause precipitation strengthening.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Facilitated dislocation transmission relieves stress concentrations that could otherwise cause premature crack initiation, thereby improving ductility.
Aging could improve yield and tensile strength by approximately 20% relative to the as-cast alloy.
Aging will increase or retain ductility while increasing strength, mitigating the strength–ductility trade-off.
The as-cast baseline lacks the refined distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates proposed for the aged condition.
Precipitate coarsening or phase instability would prevent the simultaneous improvement of strength and ductility.
The relationship among precipitate size, precipitate distribution, and eutectic microstructure may vary with alloy composition.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis and falsification rule require an increase in both strength and ductility, whereas the predicted outcome allows mere retention of ductility. Retention would satisfy the predicted outcome but fail the stated falsification criterion.
